source_text: ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΡΙΕ ΨΑΛΜΟΝ. Ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα· ἐγὼ δὲ ἐταπεινώθην σφόδρα· ἐγὼ δὲ εἶπα ἐν τῇ ἐκστάσει μου· Πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ψεύστης. Πίστις ἡγείσθω τῶν περὶ Θεοῦ λόγων· πίστις, καὶ μὴ ἀπόδειξις. Πίστις, ἡ ὑπὲρ τὰς λογικὰς μεθόδους τὴν ψυχὴν εἰς συγκατάθεσιν ἕλκουσα· πίστις, οὐχ ἡ γεωμετρικαῖς ἀνάγκαις, ἀλλ' ἡ ταῖς τοῦ Πνεύματος ἐνεργείαις ἐγ γινομένη. Ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Ναζωραίου, ἔγειραι καὶ περιπάτει. Ταύτῃ τῇ φωνῇ ἐπηκολούθει τὸ ἔργον διὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος. Ἐκ τοῦ θαύματος ἀναγκαία ἡ παραδοχὴ τῆς θεότητος τοῦ Μονογενοῦς τοῖς ὁρῶσιν ἐγίνετο. Τί ἀναγκαστικώτερον εἰς συγκατάθεσιν (εἰπέ μοι); προτάσεων πλοκαὶ τὸ συμπέρασμα ἀκόλουθον ἑαυταῖς ἐφελκόμεναι, ἢ θαῦμα τοσοῦτον ἐναργῶς ὁρώμενον, πᾶσαν ἀνθρώπου δύναμιν ὑπερβαῖνον; Ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ νῦν ταῦτα εὐδοκιμεῖ, οὐδὲ τὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος ἔργα τὸν περὶ Θεοῦ λόγον πιστοῦται· ἀλλ' ἔντεχνοι ἀπο δείξεις, ἐν τῷ πιθανῷ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου σοφίας ἔχου σαι τὴν ἐλπίδα, οὐκ ἐν τῷ ἰσχυρῷ καὶ ἐναργεῖ τῆς τοῦ Πνεύματος ἀποκαλύψεως, ἣν, διὰ τῶν ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας ἀπεριεργάστως πεποιθότων Θεῷ, τῆς σωτηρίας ἕνεκεν τῶν πολλῶν ἐπιδείκνυται. Ἀλλ' εἴθε κἀμοὶ γένοιτο πιστεῦσαι ἀξίως, ἵνα λαλήσω νῦν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῇ μεγάλῃ ταύτῃ πέντε λό γους ἐν τῷ νοΐ μου. Καὶ μηδεὶς καταχλευαζέτω τὸν λόγον, ὡς ἀβασανίστως ἡμῶν εἰς τὴν ὑπὲρ ὧν λέγομεν συγκατάθεσιν τοὺς ἀκούοντας ἐναγόντων. Ἀνάγκη γὰρ ἑκάστης μαθήσεως ἀνεξετάστους εἶναι τὰς ἀρχὰς τοῖς μανθάνουσιν· ἐπεὶ ἀμήχανον τοὺς περὶ τὰ πρῶτα ζυγομαχοῦντας δυνηθῆναι ὁδῷ καὶ τάξει προελθεῖν εἰς τὸ τέλος. Καὶ τοῦτο ἂν μάθοις παρ' αὐτῶν τῶν ἔξωθεν. Εἰ γὰρ μὴ συγχωρήσειας τὰς πρώτας ἀρχὰς τῷ γεωμέτρῃ, ἀμήχανον αὐτὸν τὰ ἐφεξῆς συμπεράνασθαι. Καὶ τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς ὁ τοῖς πρώτοις καὶ στοιχειώδεσιν ἐνιστάμενος, τὴν εἰς τὸ πρόσω ὁδὸν διακόπτει. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἰατρικαὶ ἀρχαὶ ἰατροῖς ἀναπόδεικτοι. Καὶ ὅλως, ἐν ὁποιῳδήποτε ἐπιτηδεύματι τῶν ὁδῷ καὶ τάξει προ ϊόντων ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος, ἀδύνατον τῶν πρώτων ὑποθέσεων ἀποδείξεις ἐπιζητεῖν· ἀλλ' ἀνάγκη τὰς τῶν λογικῶν τεχνῶν ἀρχὰς ἀνεξετάστως παραδεξάμενον, τὸ ἐκ τῶν ὑποτεθέντων ἀκόλουθον ἐν τοῖς ἐφεξῆς ἐπιβλέπειν. Οὕτω δὴ οὖν καὶ τὸ τῆς θεολογίας μυ στήριον, τὴν ἐκ τῆς ἀβασανίστου πίστεως ἐπιζητεῖ συγκατάθεσιν. Πιστεῦσαι γὰρ δεῖ, φησὶν, ὅτι ἔστι Θεὸς, οὐχὶ ζητῆσαι, οὐδὲ ζυγομαχῆσαι τὸ τί ἐστι. Καὶ ὅλως, εἰ ἡ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ἐστὶν ὑπόστασις πραγμάτων, καὶ ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων, μὴ φιλονείκει ἰδεῖν ἤδη τὰ μακρὰν ἀποκείμενα, μηδὲ τὰ ἐλπι ζόμενα ἀμφίβολα καταστήσῃς, διὰ τὸ μήπω αὐτῶν δύνασθαι κατὰ τὴν γνῶσιν ἐφάπτεσθαι. Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν καθόλου περὶ πίστεως διὰ τοὺς λογομαχοῦντας καὶ ἐν ῥήμασι κενοῖς ἔχοντας τὴν ἐλπίδα. Δοκεῖ δέ μοι ὁ ἐν χερσὶ ψαλμὸς ὡς πρὸς τὴν προάγουσαν ἐν τῷ κατόπιν ψαλμῷ διάνοιαν ἀκολου θίαν ἔχειν. Εἶπε γὰρ ἐκεῖ· Εὐαρεστήσω τῷ Κυρίῳ ἐν χώρᾳ ζώντων. Ἐπεὶ οὖν περὶ μὴ βλεπομένης χώρας διαλέγεται, ὡς σαφῶς ἐπιστάμενος, τὴν αἰτίαν ἀποδίδωσι τοῦ περὶ τῶν ἀδήλων διορισμοῦ, λέγων· Ἐπίστευσα, ὅτι ἔστι τις χώρα ζώντων· διὸ ἐλά λησα, ὅτι Εὐαρεστήσω ἐν αὐτῇ τῷ Κυρίῳ.
orientation: Basil opens the homily by quoting the first verse of Psalm 115 (LXX) and immediately argues that faith, not demonstration, must lead all speech about God.
pass_a_gloss: ON PSALM 115. I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was humbled greatly; but I said in my ecstasy: Every man is a liar. Let faith lead the words about God; faith, and not demonstration. Faith, the thing that draws the soul to assent beyond logical methods; faith, not the one that comes about by geometrical necessities, but the one that comes about by the energies of the Spirit. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk. To this voice the deed followed through the Spirit. From the wonder the acceptance of the divinity of the Only-begotten became necessary for those who saw. What is more compelling for assent (tell me)? The interweavings of premises drawing the conclusion that follows from them, or a wonder so great being seen clearly, surpassing every power of man? But do not these things even now have good repute, and do not the works of the Spirit give credence to the word about God? But artful demonstrations, having their hope in the persuasiveness of the wisdom of the world, not in the strong and clear thing of the revelation of the Spirit, which, through those who have trusted God in simplicity of heart without over-inquiry, is displayed for the sake of the salvation of the many. But would that it might happen also to me to believe worthily, so that I may speak now to the Church of God, this great one, five words in my mind. And let no one mock the word, as if we lead the hearers to assent about the things we say without examination. For it is necessary that the first principles of every discipline be unexamined for the learners; since it is impossible that those who dispute about the first things be able to advance by method and order to the end. And you might learn this from the outsiders themselves. For if you do not grant the first principles to the geometer, it is impossible for him to complete the things that follow. And in arithmetic, the one who opposes the first and elementary things cuts off the road forward. Likewise also the medical first principles are undemonstrated for physicians. And in general, in whatever pursuit of those who advance by method and order to the end, it is impossible to seek demonstrations of the first hypotheses; but it is necessary, having accepted the first principles of the logical arts without examination, to observe in what follows the consequence from the things hypothesized. Thus then indeed also the mystery of theology seeks the assent that comes from unexamined faith. For one must believe, he says, that God exists, not seek, nor dispute what he is. And in general, if faith is the substance of things hoped for, and the proof of things not seen, do not be contentious to see already the things stored far away, nor make the things hoped for doubtful, because it is not yet possible to grasp them according to knowledge. These things then in general about faith, for the sake of those who dispute about words and have their hope in empty words. But the psalm in hand seems to me to have a sequence with the thought that went before in the previous psalm. For he said there: I will please the Lord in the land of the living. Since therefore he speaks about a land not seen, as one who knows clearly, he gives the reason for the determination about the unseen things, saying: I believed, that there is some land of the living; therefore I spoke, that I will please the Lord in it.

choices.term: Πίστις ἡγείσθω τῶν περὶ Θεοῦ λόγων
choices.english: Let faith lead the words about God
choices.why: ἡγείσθω is a third-person imperative of ἡγέομαι, 'lead'; the genitive τῶν λόγων is the object led, preserving the command's force.
rejected: Let faith be the guide of words about God
Faith must govern speech about God

choices.term: ἡ ταῖς τοῦ Πνεύματος ἐνεργείαις ἐγγινομένη
choices.english: the one that comes about by the energies of the Spirit
choices.why: ἐγγινομένη means 'coming to be in/arising in'; the dative ταῖς ἐνεργείαις expresses means, and 'energies' is the standard patristic term for divine operations.
rejected: produced by the operations of the Spirit

choices.why: ἀβασάνιστος means 'untested, unexamined'; the adverb preserves the sense of accepting without prior scrutiny, which is Basil's point about first principles.
ζυγομαχέω means 'to fight about the yoke' or 'to quarrel over terms'; 'dispute' captures the contentious wrangling over first principles Basil condemns.
This is the classic rendering of Hebrews 11:1; 'substance' preserves the philosophical weight of ὑπόστασις that Basil exploits.
ἔλεγχος means 'proof, conviction, refutation'; 'proof' fits Basil's contrast with demonstration and preserves the forensic sense.

pass_b_english: I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was humbled exceedingly; but I said in my ecstasy, “Every man is a liar.” Let faith lead the words about God—faith, and not demonstration. Faith is what draws the soul to assent by means that surpass logical methods; faith is what comes about not by geometrical necessities but by the energies of the Spirit. “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk” (Acts 3:6). The deed followed that voice through the Spirit. From the wonder, the acceptance of the divinity of the Only-begotten became necessary for those who saw. Tell me, what is more compelling toward assent: the weaving together of propositions dragging their conclusion along after them, or a wonder so great, seen so clearly, surpassing every human power? But these things are not approved even now, nor do the works of the Spirit give credibility to the word about God. Instead, artful demonstrations hold their hope in the persuasiveness of the world’s wisdom, not in the strong and clear revelation of the Spirit, which he displays for the salvation of the many through those who have trusted God in simplicity of heart without curious inquiry. But would that I too might believe worthily, so that I may now speak five words with my mind to this great Church of God. And let no one mock the word, as though we were leading our hearers to assent about the things we say without examination. For the first principles of every discipline must necessarily be unexamined by those who learn them; otherwise it is impossible for those who dispute about the first things to advance by method and order to the end. You could learn this even from those outside. For if you do not grant the first principles to the geometer, it is impossible for him to complete what follows. And in arithmetic, the one who opposes the first and elementary principles cuts off the road ahead. Likewise, the first principles of medicine are undemonstrated for physicians. And in general, in whatever pursuit of those who advance by method and order to the end, it is impossible to seek demonstrations of the first assumptions. Rather, one must accept the first principles of the rational arts without examination, and then observe what follows from the things assumed in what comes after. So then, the mystery of theology also seeks assent from unexamined faith. For one must believe, it says, that God exists—not investigate, nor dispute what he is (Hebrews 11:6). And in general, if faith is the substance of things hoped for and the proof of things not seen (Hebrews 11:1), do not be contentious about seeing now the things stored far away, and do not make the things hoped for doubtful because you cannot yet grasp them by knowledge. These things, then, are said in general about faith for the sake of those who fight over words and hold their hope in empty phrases. Now the psalm in hand seems to me to have a sequence of thought that follows the thought of the preceding psalm. For there he said, “I will be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9 LXX; Psalm 116:9 Hebrew). Since, then, he speaks about a land not seen, as one who knows it clearly, he gives the reason for his determination about things unseen, saying: “I believed that there is a land of the living; therefore I spoke, that I will be pleasing to the Lord in it” (Psalm 115:1 LXX; Psalm 116:10 Hebrew).

problems.quote: But are not these things approved even now, nor do the works of the Spirit give credibility to the word about God.
problems.source_quote: Ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ νῦν ταῦτα εὐδοκιμεῖ, οὐδὲ τὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος ἔργα τὸν περὶ Θεοῦ λόγον πιστοῦται
problems.why: Greek says 'these things are NOT approved now, NOR do the works of the Spirit give credibility'—both negated. English 'But are not...nor' flips to a question expecting 'yes they are,' changing Basil's lament that signs no longer win approval to a claim that they still do.
problems.fix: But these things are not approved even now, nor do the works of the Spirit give credibility to the word about God.
